```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(ggplot2)
```

*Getting started* (`vignette("fmriAR-introduction")`) ran the default
workflow on noise that matched its assumptions. This vignette covers the
choices behind that workflow: why to pass the design to `fit_noise()`, how
the AR order is chosen and how to tell when it is too low, standard errors
that tolerate leftover autocorrelation, when an ARMA model fits better, and
how to use filters specified in AFNI's restricted form.

The examples use the same kind of simulated study as *Getting started*: two
runs of 150 volumes at a TR of 2 seconds, an event-related task, and an
intercept and a set of cosine drift terms for each run. Each section changes
the noise; the first also varies the number of drift terms.

```{r helpers}
library(fmriAR)
set.seed(7)

TR <- 2
n_per_run <- 150
runs <- rep(1:2, each = n_per_run)
n_time <- length(runs)

hrf <- function(t) dgamma(t, 6) - dgamma(t, 16) / 6
h <- hrf(seq(0, 30, by = TR))
event_regressor <- function(n) {
  onsets <- cumsum(sample(6:10, n, replace = TRUE))
  stim <- tabulate(onsets[onsets <= n], nbins = n)
  x <- stats::filter(stim, h / max(h), sides = 1)
  as.numeric(replace(x, is.na(x), 0))
}
cosines <- function(n, k) {
  sapply(seq_len(k), function(j) cos(pi * j * (seq_len(n) - 0.5) / n))
}

# Task, one intercept per run, and k cosine drift terms per run
make_design <- function(k = 3) {
  X <- cbind(task = c(event_regressor(n_per_run), event_regressor(n_per_run)),
             run1 = runs == 1, run2 = runs == 2)
  if (k > 0) {
    none <- matrix(0, n_per_run, k)
    X <- cbind(X, rbind(cosines(n_per_run, k), none),
                  rbind(none, cosines(n_per_run, k)))
  }
  X
}

# Noise for n_vox voxels, each run simulated separately: an AR process with
# coefficients `ar`, plus optional white noise with standard deviation white_sd
simulate_noise <- function(n_vox, ar, white_sd = 0) {
  one_run <- function() {
    as.numeric(arima.sim(list(ar = ar), n = n_per_run)) +
      rnorm(n_per_run, sd = white_sd)
  }
  replicate(n_vox, c(one_run(), one_run()))
}
```

```{r acf-helpers, include = FALSE}
# Plot for the whiteness check: per-lag voxel ranges against per-lag bands
check_frame <- function(chk, stage) {
  data.frame(stage = stage, lag = seq_len(nrow(chk$ac)),
             lo = apply(chk$ac, 1, quantile, 0.025),
             mid = apply(chk$ac, 1, median),
             hi = apply(chk$ac, 1, quantile, 0.975),
             band_lo = chk$band[1, ], band_hi = chk$band[2, ],
             outside = chk$outside)
}
plot_acf_check <- function(acs, good, label_stage) {
  acs$status <- ifelse(acs$stage %in% good, "Whitened", "OLS")
  lab <- subset(acs, stage == label_stage & lag <= 2)
  lab$txt <- sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * lab$outside)
  # Put each label beyond the end of its line that leaves the band
  up <- lab$mid > 0
  lab$y <- ifelse(up, lab$hi, lab$lo)
  lab$vj <- ifelse(up, -0.4, 1.4)
  lab$hj <- ifelse(lab$lag == 1, 0.2, 0.5)       # keep lag 1 inside the panel
  ggplot(acs, aes(lag)) +
    geom_rect(aes(xmin = lag - 0.38, xmax = lag + 0.38,
                  ymin = band_lo, ymax = band_hi), fill = "grey88") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey55") +
    geom_linerange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi, colour = status), linewidth = 0.6) +
    geom_point(aes(y = mid, colour = status), size = 1.7) +
    geom_text(data = lab, aes(x = lag, y = y, label = txt, vjust = vj, hjust = hj),
              size = 2.9, colour = "grey30") +
    facet_wrap(~stage, nrow = 1) +
    albersdown::scale_color_albers(limits = c("Whitened", "OLS"), guide = "none") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 4, 8)) +
    scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.12, 0.12))) +
    labs(x = "Lag (volumes)", y = "Autocorrelation") +
    theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
          strip.text = element_text(hjust = 0),
          panel.grid.major = element_blank())
}
```

## Why `design = X` matters

The noise model is estimated from residuals, and residuals are not the noise.
Fitting a model removes from the data whatever the regressors can
reproduce, and that includes some of the noise. In matrix terms the residuals
are $My$, where $M = I - X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top$ is the projection that
removes the design, so their covariance is $M \Sigma M$ rather than the
noise covariance $\Sigma$.

The result is a downward bias in the estimated autocorrelation, and drift
terms cause most of it: slow cosines soak up slow fluctuations, which is
where autocorrelated noise keeps its power. Below, the same AR(1) noise,
with coefficient 0.5, is fitted under designs with more and more drift
terms, once without the design (`plain`) and once with it (`corrected`).

```{r bias}
noise <- simulate_noise(2000, ar = 0.5)

n_drift <- c(0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12)
bias <- t(sapply(n_drift, function(k) {
  X_k <- make_design(k)
  r <- lm.fit(X_k, noise)$residuals
  c(drift_terms = k,
    plain = fit_noise(r, runs = runs, p = 1)$phi[[1]],
    corrected = fit_noise(r, runs = runs, p = 1, design = X_k)$phi[[1]])
}))
round(bias, 3)
```

```{r fig-bias, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.2, fig.cap = "Estimated AR(1) coefficient as drift terms are added to the design. The noise is the same throughout, and its true coefficient is 0.5. Without the design, the estimate falls steadily; with design = X, it stays at the truth through 8 drift terms per run. The examples in these vignettes use 3."}
bd <- data.frame(k = rep(bias[, "drift_terms"], 2),
                 phi = c(bias[, "plain"], bias[, "corrected"]),
                 fit = rep(c("OLS", "Whitened"), each = nrow(bias)))
lab <- data.frame(k = 6, phi = c(bias[bias[, "drift_terms"] == 6, "plain"] - 0.012,
                                 0.5 + 0.012),
                  txt = c("without design", "with design = X"))
ggplot(bd, aes(k, phi, colour = fit)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 3, linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey85") +
  annotate("text", x = 3.2, y = min(bias[, "plain"]), label = "used in\nthese examples",
           hjust = 0, vjust = 0, size = 2.8, lineheight = 0.9, colour = "grey45") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linewidth = 0.4, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  geom_text(data = lab, aes(k, phi, label = txt), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            hjust = c(1, 0.5), vjust = c(1, 0), size = 3.1, colour = "grey25") +
  albersdown::scale_color_albers(limits = c("Whitened", "OLS"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = n_drift) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0.35, 0.4, 0.45, 0.5),
                     labels = c("0.35", "0.40", "0.45", "0.50 truth")) +
  labs(x = "Cosine drift terms per run", y = "Estimated coefficient") +
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank())
```

`design = X` corrects for the projection: `fit_noise()` works out the bias
that $M$ puts into each lag of the autocovariance and inverts it. The
correction works with every pooling mode for AR models, and with censoring.
It needs residuals that really are OLS residuals from `X`; a numerical check
rejects obvious mismatches.

From 10 cosine terms per run the corrected estimate starts to slip. Ten
cosines in a 150-volume run amount to a 60-second high-pass filter, far
stricter than the usual 128 seconds. The correction is computed up to a lag
budget, `correction_max_lag` (default 25), and with that many drift terms
the longer budget makes it less stable. Nothing warns of this. A shorter
budget that still covers the noise's autocorrelation fixes it:

```{r lag-budget}
X_12 <- make_design(12)
r_12 <- lm.fit(X_12, noise)$residuals
c(default = fit_noise(r_12, runs = runs, p = 1, design = X_12)$phi[[1]],
  budget_10 = fit_noise(r_12, runs = runs, p = 1, design = X_12,
                        correction_max_lag = 10)$phi[[1]])
```

If refitting with a shorter budget changes the estimate, use the shorter
budget.

Two helpers expose the same correction. `noise_acvf(resid, design = X)`
returns the corrected autocovariance itself. `acvf_bias_matrix()` builds the
correction once, so that it can be passed to `fit_noise(acvf_correction = )`
for many datasets that share the same design, run structure and censored
volumes.

## Choosing the AR order

With `p = "auto"` (the default), `fit_noise()` tries every order from 0 to
`p_max` (default 6) and keeps the one with the lowest Bayesian information
criterion (BIC). Pooling many voxels gives BIC more evidence than one series
would. But neighbouring voxels share fluctuations, so `fit_noise()` counts
them as an effective number of independent voxels,
$V / (1 + (V - 1)\bar r)$ for $V$ voxels with mean inter-voxel correlation
$\bar r$. That count is deliberately conservative.

The design correction matters here too. Projection bias distorts every lag a
little, and with thousands of voxels BIC treats those small, systematic
distortions as structure worth extra coefficients. Here the noise is AR(2):

```{r order}
X <- make_design(3)
noise_ar2 <- simulate_noise(2000, ar = c(0.4, 0.2))
r_ar2 <- lm.fit(X, noise_ar2)$residuals

p_without <- fit_noise(r_ar2, runs = runs)$order[["p"]]
p_with <- fit_noise(r_ar2, runs = runs, design = X)$order[["p"]]
c(without_design = p_without, with_design = p_with)
```

With the design, the search finds AR(`r p_with`). Without it, the search
chooses AR(`r p_without`), adding `r p_without - p_with` coefficients that
describe the projection, not the noise.

### Spotting an order that is too low

The whiteness check from *Getting started* shows when an order is too low.
Here it is as two functions: `whitened()` refits a noise model's whitened
data and returns the residuals with the whitened design, and `whiteness()`
compares each voxel's autocorrelations with the white-noise band for that
design, built by passing pure white noise through the same fit.

```{r whiteness}
white <- matrix(rnorm(n_time * 2000), n_time)

whitened <- function(plan, Y) {
  w <- whiten_apply(plan, X, Y, runs = runs)
  list(resid = w$Y - w$X %*% qr.coef(qr(w$X), w$Y), design = w$X)
}
whiteness <- function(resid, design, max_lag = 8) {
  ac <- acorr_diagnostics(resid, runs = runs, max_lag = max_lag,
                          aggregate = "none")$acf
  ref <- acorr_diagnostics(qr.resid(qr(design), white), runs = runs,
                           max_lag = max_lag, aggregate = "none")$acf
  band <- apply(ref, 1, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
  list(ac = ac, band = band,
       outside = rowMeans(ac < band[1, ] | ac > band[2, ]))   # share per lag
}
```

Below, the same AR(2) noise is whitened twice: with an AR(1) model, and with
the AR(2) model the search chose.

```{r underfit}
plan_ar1 <- fit_noise(r_ar2, runs = runs, p = 1, design = X)
plan_ar2 <- fit_noise(r_ar2, runs = runs, design = X)
w_ar1 <- whitened(plan_ar1, noise_ar2)
w_ar2 <- whitened(plan_ar2, noise_ar2)

# The order chosen without the design correction, for comparison
plan_nodesign <- fit_noise(r_ar2, runs = runs)
w_nod <- whitened(plan_nodesign, noise_ar2)

# Share of voxels outside the band at lags 1 to 3
round(rbind(
  `AR(1) fit` = whiteness(w_ar1$resid, w_ar1$design)$outside[1:3],
  `AR(2) fit` = whiteness(w_ar2$resid, w_ar2$design)$outside[1:3],
  `AR(6), no design` = whiteness(w_nod$resid, w_nod$design)$outside[1:3]
), 3)
```

White noise leaves 5% outside; with 2,000 voxels, chance moves that share by
about 1.5 points either way. The AR(1) filter fails at lags 1 and 2: it
overshoots at lag 1, turning a strong positive autocorrelation negative, and
leaves a positive one at lag 2. The AR(2) filter passes. The AR(6) filter
chosen without the design correction fails too, more mildly: its extra
coefficients fit the projection's distortion, and whitening with them
leaves autocorrelation behind.

```{r fig-underfit, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.3, fig.cap = "The whiteness check for AR(2) noise: residual autocorrelation after OLS, after an AR(1) filter and after an AR(2) filter. Lines span the middle 95% of voxels; dots mark the median; grey boxes are the white-noise band for each fit. The AR(1) filter fails at lags 1 and 2, where the percentages give the share of voxels outside the band; the AR(2) filter passes."}
lev <- c("OLS", "AR(1) fit", "AR(2) fit")
acs <- rbind(check_frame(whiteness(r_ar2, X), lev[1]),
             check_frame(whiteness(w_ar1$resid, w_ar1$design), lev[2]),
             check_frame(whiteness(w_ar2$resid, w_ar2$design), lev[3]))
acs$stage <- factor(acs$stage, levels = lev)
plot_acf_check(acs, good = lev[3], label_stage = lev[2])
```

## Robust standard errors

By default (`type = "iid"`), `sandwich_from_whitened_resid()` returns the
ordinary standard error, which assumes the whitened noise is white. When
some autocorrelation survives whitening, that standard error is off again,
in a direction that depends on what was missed. `type = "hac"` gives a
heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent (HAC) Newey–West
estimator, computed within runs, which allows for leftover autocorrelation
at short lags. `type = "hc0"` allows for unequal variances only.

The AR(2) noise above has no task effect, so every voxel is null and 5% of
them should pass $|t| > 1.96$:

```{r robust}
false_positive_rate <- function(plan, type) {
  w <- whiten_apply(plan, X, noise_ar2, runs = runs)
  fit <- lm.fit(w$X, w$Y)
  se <- sandwich_from_whitened_resid(w$X, w$Y, beta = fit$coefficients,
                                     type = type, runs = runs)$se
  mean(abs(fit$coefficients["task", ] / se[1, ]) > 1.96)
}
rates <- sapply(c("iid", "hac"), function(type) {
  c(`AR(1), too low` = false_positive_rate(plan_ar1, type),
    `AR(2), correct` = false_positive_rate(plan_ar2, type))
})
knitr::kable(rates, digits = 3,
             caption = "Share of null voxels with |t| > 1.96, by noise model and standard error.")
```

With the AR(1) model, the ordinary standard error is wrong. Here it errs on
the cautious side; other misfits make it err the other way. HAC brings the
rate back toward 5%, and with the correct AR(2) model the two agree. Use HAC
as a safety net when a noise model cannot pass the whiteness check, not as a
substitute for a good noise model. It has no small-sample correction, so in
short runs it is approximate.

## ARMA models

Scanner noise adds white noise on top of the autocorrelated physiological
noise. An AR(1) process plus white noise is no longer AR(1): it is
ARMA(1,1), with one autoregressive and one moving-average coefficient. A pure
AR model can mimic it only with extra coefficients. Below, the noise is
AR(1) with coefficient 0.8 plus white noise. The design correction is
available for AR models only, so the ARMA fit omits `design` and carries the
projection bias.

```{r arma}
noise_mix <- simulate_noise(2000, ar = 0.8, white_sd = 1)
r_mix <- lm.fit(X, noise_mix)$residuals

plan_ar_auto <- fit_noise(r_mix, runs = runs, design = X)
plan_arma <- fit_noise(r_mix, runs = runs, method = "arma", p = 1, q = 1)

plan_ar_auto$order
plan_arma
```

ARMA models are estimated by the Hannan–Rissanen procedure, pooled over
voxels: each voxel is a replicate series sharing the coefficients, and no
lag crosses a run boundary or a censored volume. `hr_iter` adds refinement
iterations. The AR coefficient comes out at
`r sprintf("%.2f", plan_arma$phi[[1]])` rather than 0.8, partly because of
the uncorrected projection bias.

The BIC search picked AR(`r plan_ar_auto$order[["p"]]`); ARMA(1,1)
describes the same noise with two coefficients. The table scores each model,
along with a plain AR(1) for comparison, by the share of voxels outside the
white-noise band at lags 1 to 3 (white noise leaves 5%) and by the
false-positive rate.

```{r arma-compare}
score <- function(plan) {
  wh <- whitened(plan, noise_mix)
  w <- whiten_apply(plan, X, noise_mix, runs = runs)
  fit <- lm.fit(w$X, w$Y)
  se <- sandwich_from_whitened_resid(w$X, w$Y, beta = fit$coefficients)$se
  c(whiteness(wh$resid, wh$design, max_lag = 3)$outside,
    mean(abs(fit$coefficients["task", ] / se[1, ]) > 1.96))
}
plan_ar1_mix <- fit_noise(r_mix, runs = runs, p = 1, design = X)
tab <- rbind(`AR(1)` = score(plan_ar1_mix),
             `AR, order by BIC` = score(plan_ar_auto),
             `ARMA(1,1)` = score(plan_arma))
colnames(tab) <- c("outside, lag 1", "lag 2", "lag 3", "false positive")
knitr::kable(tab, digits = 3,
             caption = "Share of voxels outside the white-noise band, and false-positive rate, for AR(1) noise plus white noise.")
```

The AR(1) fails clearly. The design-corrected AR model passes. ARMA(1,1)
fails at lags 1 and 2, with
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * tab["ARMA(1,1)", 1])` and
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * tab["ARMA(1,1)", 2])` of voxels outside the band.
Without the design correction its coefficients carry the projection bias,
and the filter leaves autocorrelation behind; with no drift terms in the
design, the same ARMA(1,1) fit passes. Its false-positive rate stays near
5% here, while the AR(1)'s tests are badly conservative. Because ARMA fits
cannot use the design correction, prefer a design-corrected AR model
whenever the design has drift terms, which is almost always.

`method = "arma"` also accepts `p = "auto"` and `q = "auto"`, which search
`0:p_max` and `0:q_max` by BIC. Do not rely on that search:

```{r arma-auto}
rbind(
  residuals = fit_noise(r_mix, runs = runs, method = "arma",
                        p = "auto", q = "auto")$order,
  noise_itself = fit_noise(noise_mix, runs = runs, method = "arma",
                           p = "auto", q = "auto")$order
)
```

On the residuals it returns the largest orders it is allowed. On the noise
itself, with no fitted model in the way, it still returns more coefficients
than the ARMA(1,1) truth. The BIC is computed on a regression that uses
estimated innovations, and with hundreds of thousands of observations the
error in that approximation looks like structure. Set the orders.

## AFNI-style restricted filters

AFNI specifies some noise models by their poles rather than their
coefficients: an AR(3) with one real pole `a` and one complex pair (radius
`r1`, angle `t1`), or an AR(5) with a second pair (`r2`, `t2`), plus an
optional share of white noise. The poles are reciprocal roots of the AR
polynomial, so values below 1 mean a stationary process. AFNI's
`1dgenARMA11` uses this form to simulate noise. `afni_restricted_plan()`
turns such a specification into an ordinary plan that `whiten_apply()` can
use. It does not estimate the poles; you supply them. The residuals passed
to it set the run structure and, with `estimate_ma1 = TRUE`, the MA term;
with `estimate_ma1 = FALSE` their values are not used.

```{r afni}
roots <- list(a = 0.5, r1 = 0.4, t1 = pi / 3)
plan_afni <- afni_restricted_plan(r_ar2, runs = runs, p = 3L, roots = roots,
                                  estimate_ma1 = FALSE)
round(plan_afni$phi[[1]], 3)
```

`a`, `r1` and `r2` must be non-negative; values above 0.95 are clamped to
0.95, and angles are clamped to $[0, \pi]$. The white noise is set by `vrt`,
the share of variance carried by the AR part. With `vrt` below 1 and
`estimate_ma1 = FALSE`, the plan is the exact ARMA(p, p) equivalent of AR(p)
plus white noise: its autocorrelation is `vrt` times the AR autocorrelation
at every nonzero lag.

```{r afni-vrt}
plan_afni_vrt <- afni_restricted_plan(r_ar2, runs = runs, p = 3L,
                                      roots = c(roots, vrt = 0.8),
                                      estimate_ma1 = FALSE)
plan_afni_vrt$order
```

With `estimate_ma1 = TRUE` (the default), the poles fix the AR part, an MA(1)
term is estimated from the AR-filtered residuals, and `vrt` is ignored. To
give each parcel its own filter, pass `parcels` and a list of pole
specifications keyed by parcel ID.
